text: The design decisions are made. Now they need to become a real deliverable someone can actually review — diagrams with real content, and a written decision record, not a drawing tool exercise.

The first diagram makes Lesson 30's structure visible: one instance, the Meridian corporate domain on top, St. Catherine's, Lakeshore, and Prairie View beneath it. A reviewer should be able to answer two questions just by looking at it. Can a Lakeshore agent see a St. Catherine's incident? No. Can a Meridian executive see across all three for a board report? Yes. If it can't answer both of those at a glance, it isn't finished — and which tool you drew it in barely matters compared to getting that content right.

The second diagram captures the integration architecture as flows, not a list: Workday syncing in event-driven, ADP answering a live request-response lookup, and Prairie View's PeopleSoft module arriving through a MID Server batch pull. Each arrow carries direction, pattern, and — critically — which domain the resulting record lands in, so a reviewer can trace a record and catch a missing domain assignment on paper, before anything gets built.

The third diagram overlays the security design: it marks the regulated zone — health-related leave cases, patient-care-unit facilities records — and marks the one place data legitimately has to cross a domain boundary, like corporate HR reviewing an aggregated leave trend across all three systems. That crossing point is exactly where the strictest controls need to live, and a security reviewer needs to find it without hunting through pages of prose.

Then comes the Architecture Decision Record. It states the context honestly: three merging hospital systems, no data-residency requirement, no real independence, but a genuine cultural need for separation. It lists the options actually weighed — three instances, one instance with no domains, or one instance with domain separation — and says plainly why the first two were rejected, not just that the third was chosen. And it states the consequences honestly: every future script and integration now has to be domain-aware, permanently, a cost accepted deliberately because the alternatives were worse.

That's what separates a real architecture deliverable from a slide full of bullet points — anyone finding this two years from now can reconstruct not just what was built, but why. Next, that reasoning gets tested out loud, in front of a panel that pushes back on every one of these choices.
